paragraphs: AccuQuant addresses a problem that arises when diffusion models are converted to lower numerical precision after training. These models generate samples through repeated denoising, so an error introduced at one step can influence later steps. The paper supports this accumulation effect with both analysis and experiments, making the full sampling process central to its quantization approach.

The method calibrates the quantized model by explicitly simulating several connected denoising steps and comparing its outputs with those of the full-precision model. This lets calibration account for errors carried forward through sampling. Previous approaches described in the abstract compare steps independently, which does not directly capture how their errors combine over time.

The paper also introduces an implementation technique and objective that reduce memory complexity from linear to constant in the number of denoising steps. Evaluations across multiple tasks and diffusion models support its effectiveness and efficiency. The contribution is therefore both a better match between quantization and actual generation, and a way to make that calibration computationally practical.
neurips-2025-accuquant-simulating-multip.tldr: AccuQuant calibrates quantized diffusion models across connected denoising steps to address accumulating errors with constant memory complexity.

paragraphs: AceReason-Nemotron investigates how reinforcement learning can improve strong small and medium-sized reasoning models. The paper focuses on the training recipe, including the order of tasks, the quality of verification data, and how updates are performed. Its experiments show that large-scale reinforcement learning can improve these models beyond the distillation-based alternatives evaluated.

The proposed sequence trains on mathematics prompts first and programming prompts afterward. Mathematics-only training also improves code reasoning: the reported gains for 7B and 14B models are 14.6% and 17.2% on AIME 2025, and 6.8% and 5.8% on LiveCodeBench. Additional code-only training improves programming results further while producing little deterioration in mathematics performance.

The authors build a data pipeline for challenging prompts with verifiable answers and test cases. Their ablations also identify benefits from progressively increasing response lengths and the stabilizing role of on-policy updates. In the studied settings, reinforcement learning enables solutions to previously unsolved problems, supporting the claim that it can extend demonstrated reasoning ability beyond simply drawing out existing successful responses.
neurips-2025-acereason-nemotron-advancin.tldr: A mathematics-first, code-second reinforcement learning recipe substantially improves strong 7B and 14B reasoning models.

paragraphs: This paper connects two ways of studying computational difficulty in statistical detection. The Franz-Parisi criterion approaches the problem through geometric overlap structure inspired by statistical physics. Statistical Query lower bounds provide another framework for establishing difficulty in statistical inference. Earlier work linked the original criterion to low-degree polynomial lower bounds for Gaussian additive models.

The authors refine the Franz-Parisi criterion to capture overlap geometry more effectively. Their main theorem establishes equivalence between this optimized criterion and Statistical Query lower bounds under a mild, verifiable assumption. That qualification matters: the equivalence is conditional, although the abstract identifies a broad collection of models satisfying the assumption.

The covered settings include Gaussian additive and planted sparse models, non-Gaussian component analysis, single-index models, and convex truncation detection. For convex truncation, the assumption is equivalent to the Gaussian correlation inequality. The connection simplifies several established lower-bound arguments and produces new bounds for mixed sparse linear regression and convex truncation. Its value is a shared route to complexity results across several statistical problems.
neurips-2025-an-optimized-franz-parisi-c.tldr: An optimized Franz-Parisi criterion matches Statistical Query lower bounds under a verifiable assumption covering many statistical models.

paragraphs: ARIA addresses a learning problem for agents that act through unrestricted language. In negotiation or question-asking games, many different token sequences can express useful actions. Searching this enormous space can produce sparse rewards and highly variable training signals, making reinforcement learning less effective even when several utterances have similar meanings.

The method groups language actions by intention. It projects actions into a lower-dimensional space, clusters semantically similar actions, and assigns shared rewards within those groups. This changes the level at which feedback is aggregated: related expressions can contribute to a common signal instead of being treated entirely separately. The aim is to make reward information denser and reduce the variance that disrupts policy optimization.

Across four downstream tasks, including negotiation and text-based games, the authors report significantly lower gradient variance and an average performance improvement of 9.95%. ARIA also outperforms the strong offline and online reinforcement learning baselines evaluated. These findings support intention-based reward sharing as a practical way to improve learning in the tested open-ended language environments.
neurips-2025-aria-training-language-agen.tldr: ARIA shares rewards among language actions with similar intentions, reducing training variance and improving performance across four tasks.

paragraphs: Auto-Compressing Networks change how layers connect in a deep neural network. Instead of traditional short residual connections, each layer contributes through an additive connection to the output. The paper studies how this architectural change alters gradient-descent training, addressing the possibility that additional depth introduces computation without a corresponding improvement in representations.

The central property is auto-compression: during training, useful information moves into earlier layers, improving their representations and exposing redundancy deeper in the network. The authors theoretically connect this behavior to layer-specific training patterns in ACNs. Layers are used dynamically according to task requirements, so the architecture itself shapes where learned information becomes concentrated.

The reported experiments find greater noise robustness, better performance with limited data, improved transfer learning, and reduced catastrophic forgetting compared with residual networks. Across vision transformers, MLP-mixers, and BERT architectures, the results include 30–80% architectural compression while preserving accuracy and up to an 18% reduction in forgetting. These findings suggest that the changed connections can support both compact architectures and useful representations.
neurips-2025-auto-compressing-networks-c.tldr: Auto-Compressing Networks use long connections to concentrate information in early layers, enabling substantial compression while maintaining tested accuracy.

paragraphs: CQN-AS asks whether predicting action sequences, an approach that has helped behavior cloning in robotics, can also benefit reinforcement learning. Its starting observation concerns prediction of return-to-go, the reward still to be accumulated. Including an action sequence when predicting that quantity produces lower validation loss in the authors' study.

Motivated by this result, the paper introduces a value-based reinforcement learning algorithm whose critic assigns Q-values to sequences of actions. The critic is the component that estimates how valuable a choice will be. Here, its explicit training target concerns the consequences of executing a sequence, making multi-action behavior part of the value representation rather than leaving that relationship implicit.

The authors evaluate CQN-AS on sparse-reward humanoid control and tabletop manipulation tasks from BiGym and RLBench. It outperforms several baselines across these tasks. Together, the predictive observation and control results support the usefulness of sequence-aware value learning in the tested settings, extending an idea associated with learning from demonstrations into reinforcement learning.
neurips-2025-coarse-to-fine-q-network-wi.tldr: CQN-AS learns values for action sequences and outperforms several baselines on sparse-reward robotic control tasks.

paragraphs: Energy-based generator matching trains generative models from an energy function without requiring a dataset of examples. The energy function supplies the target information from which the model learns to sample. The paper aims to make this approach applicable across different kinds of variables, rather than restricting it to a single data modality.

The method extends generator matching to train continuous-time Markov processes, including diffusion, flow, and jump processes. Its supported state spaces include continuous variables, discrete variables, and combinations of the two. This breadth matters because a common training approach can cover generation problems with fundamentally different kinds of possible outcomes.

To estimate the training loss, the authors use self-normalized importance sampling and add a bootstrapping technique that reduces variance in the importance weights. This addresses a statistical difficulty in learning from the energy-based target. Experiments validate the method on discrete tasks reaching 100 dimensions and multimodal tasks reaching 20 dimensions. Those results provide empirical support for the framework in the tested settings alongside its broader methodological formulation.
neurips-2025-energy-based-generator-matc.tldr: Energy-based generator matching learns samplers from energy functions without training data across continuous, discrete, and mixed state spaces.

paragraphs: FARAD addresses a feedback problem in semi-supervised learning: incorrect labels predicted for unlabeled examples can reinforce a classifier's preference for majority classes. Some bias-correction methods probe the classifier using blank or uniformly colored images. The paper argues that these references poorly reflect real data statistics, which can make the estimated bias inaccurate.

FARAD constructs reference images by retaining the Fourier amplitude spectrum of real images while randomizing their phase. The intended combination is realistic statistical characteristics without recognizable semantic content. Preserved amplitudes retain relevant texture, color, and frequency information, while phase randomization removes structural cues. The classifier's responses to these references are then used to estimate per-class biases.

The approach is grounded in Fourier analysis, and an optimized batched real-to-complex FFT implementation improves computational efficiency. Experiments report significant gains in minority-class accuracy and overall semi-supervised performance relative to existing reference-based correction methods, especially under difficult imbalance conditions. The findings support the importance of choosing statistically representative reference inputs when estimating and correcting classifier bias.
neurips-2025-fourier-clouds-fast-bias-co.tldr: FARAD uses Fourier-based reference images to estimate classifier bias and improve imbalanced semi-supervised learning.

paragraphs: HairFree generates complete bald-head textures from textual descriptions using a diffusion prior learned from mostly frontal face images. It addresses the challenge of producing a consistent appearance around an entire head when expensive, carefully tracked multi-view training data are unavailable. The method also supports detailed non-human skin appearances.

The diffusion prior is fine-tuned with predicted head geometry and face-region information. At generation time, precise skin masks and 3D FLAME geometry condition the process. HairFree first produces a frontal image aligned with the head pose, maps it into UV texture space, and then moves a virtual camera around the head while filling and merging previously unseen regions.

A semantic prior separates regions, particularly hair from skin, so the resulting bald texture can be combined with customizable hair and other accessories. The abstract reports that training requires no texture, back-view, bald, non-human, or synthetic data. Quantitative and qualitative evaluations show advantages over the compared head-avatar generation methods, supporting the use of compositional 2D priors for consistent full-head texturing.
neurips-2025-hairfree-compositional-2d-h.tldr: HairFree turns text descriptions and mostly frontal-face training data into consistent 360-degree bald-head textures.

paragraphs: HypoBootstrap gives language models a structured procedure for inferring general rules from evidence. The paper identifies a tradeoff in earlier approaches: formal-language methods require difficult conversions, while direct language-model generation can hallucinate and lacks systematic guidance. Its framework organizes both the creation of hypotheses and their subsequent confirmation.

Hypothesis generation proceeds through three stages: object hypotheses, relational hypotheses, and functional hypotheses. This sequence helps the model move from simpler observed patterns toward more complex ones. The bootstrapping structure makes increasingly rich hypotheses part of an ordered reasoning process, rather than asking the model to produce a complete explanation in one unconstrained step.

For confirmation, the framework applies principles from Glymour's bootstrap confirmation theory, which can evaluate sets of hypotheses. These principles are used across all three hypothesis categories. Empirical studies cover causal induction, concept learning, grammar learning, and abstract reasoning, with significant improvements over existing methods. The findings support combining staged hypothesis construction with a dedicated confirmation procedure across several distinct forms of inductive reasoning.
neurips-2025-hypobootstrap-a-bootstrappi.tldr: HypoBootstrap improves inductive reasoning by systematically building and confirming object, relational, and functional hypotheses.

paragraphs: INC studies hybrid simulation methods that combine a coarse numerical solver with a learned correction. Applying corrections directly to the solver's output can introduce perturbations that become amplified as predictions feed into later simulation steps. The paper's theoretical framework identifies this accumulated error as especially problematic for long simulations and chaotic systems.

The proposed alternative inserts learned corrections into the governing equations instead of directly changing the predicted state. The analysis relates its reduction in error amplification to the timestep and a Lipschitz constant. The framework imposes no neural architecture requirements, allowing the correction strategy to be combined with different networks and numerical solvers.

Experiments span differentiable solvers, neural backbones, and systems ranging from one-dimensional chaos to three-dimensional turbulence. The reported results include up to 158.7% improvement in long-term trajectory R², stabilization under aggressive coarsening, and speedups of several orders of magnitude for complex 3D turbulence cases. These findings support changing where corrections enter the simulation as a route to more stable and efficient learned PDE solvers.
neurips-2025-inc-an-indirect-neural-corr.tldr: INC incorporates neural corrections into governing equations to reduce error amplification and improve long-term PDE simulations.

paragraphs: MEIcoder reconstructs viewed images from activity recorded in primary visual cortex. The paper focuses on situations where neural recordings and training examples are scarce, a significant obstacle for deep learning decoders. Its approach incorporates neuron-specific most exciting inputs, or MEIs, which describe visual inputs that strongly excite individual neurons.

The decoder combines these MEIs with a structural-similarity loss and adversarial training. This brings information about individual neurons' visual preferences into the reconstruction process. Ablation experiments identify MEIs as the main source of the performance gains, giving evidence that the biologically informed component plays a central role in the method's results.

The authors report state-of-the-art reconstruction performance, particularly with smaller datasets and fewer recorded neurons. Scaling experiments produce high-fidelity, natural-looking images using 1,000–2,500 neurons and fewer than 1,000 training examples. They also introduce a unified benchmark containing over 160,000 samples. Together, the results support visual decoding in the studied early-visual-system setting and provide a larger shared resource for evaluating future reconstruction methods.
neurips-2025-meicoder-decoding-visual-st.tldr: MEIcoder uses neuron-specific preferred inputs to reconstruct visual stimuli effectively from limited neural recordings and training data.

paragraphs: SpatialNavigator helps vision-language models reason about how a scene changes when the observer moves. The paper identifies a gap between interpreting a two-dimensional image and anticipating three-dimensional scene dynamics. It addresses that gap by connecting the vision-language model to a controllable world model based on video diffusion.

During inference, the vision-language model proposes a short camera trajectory. The world model synthesizes views along that trajectory, and the vision-language model uses the resulting perspectives as additional evidence. This process repeats interactively, turning spatial reasoning into an exploration procedure. Extra computation at test time is used to generate and inspect views relevant to the question.

Without fine-tuning, the method achieves a reported average performance improvement of 7.7% on the SAT spatial reasoning benchmark. It also improves upon the evaluated test-time inference models trained through reinforcement learning. These results support coupling language-and-vision reasoning with generated multi-view evidence as a practical way to improve spatial reasoning in the tested tasks.
neurips-2025-mindjourney-test-time-scali.tldr: SpatialNavigator improves spatial reasoning without fine-tuning by letting a vision-language model explore views generated by a world model.

paragraphs: PhyBlock evaluates whether vision-language models understand physical scenes well enough to plan three-dimensional block assembly. Its focus extends beyond recognizing objects to reasoning about their properties, spatial relationships, and the scene as a whole. The benchmark organizes assembly tasks into a four-level cognitive hierarchy so that performance can be examined as reasoning demands increase.

The dataset contains 2,600 tasks: 400 assembly tasks and 2,200 visual question-answering tasks. Evaluation considers partial completion, failure diagnosis, and planning robustness. These complementary views examine how much a model accomplishes, whether it can identify what went wrong, and how dependable its planning is within the benchmark.

Testing 23 vision-language models reveals pronounced weaknesses in higher-level planning and reasoning, with performance declining as tasks become more complex. Error analysis highlights persistent problems with spatial orientation and dependency reasoning. The contribution is a unified testbed that makes these difficulties visible through both targeted questions and multi-step assembly, providing evidence about where physically grounded reasoning remains challenging.
neurips-2025-phyblock-a-progressive-benc.tldr: PhyBlock tests physical reasoning through 3D block assembly and reveals substantial planning weaknesses across 23 vision-language models.

paragraphs: This paper develops a theoretical approach to diffusion training when a few classes dominate the data and many others have few examples. Its objective combines the usual diffusion loss with a mutual-learning term intended to support balanced performance across labels. The goal includes underrepresented classes rather than focusing only on aggregate performance.

The authors formulate training as a multiplayer game and use Nash equilibrium as the solution concept. They derive a finite-iteration convergence result for individual gradient descent. Specifically, the Nash gap is bounded by an expression of order 1/√T_train + β, where T_train counts training iterations and β controls regularization. The bound therefore reflects both training progress and the chosen regularization strength.

Under the paper's model, the authors also establish training and sampling hyperparameters yielding a worst-case sampling-error bound of order ε + 1 across all class labels, for any positive ε. This stated bound retains a constant term. The contribution is a mathematical framework connecting imbalanced diffusion training, game-based optimization, and class-wide sampling guarantees.
neurips-2025-principled-long-tailed-gene.tldr: A game-theoretic diffusion objective provides convergence and class-wide sampling-error guarantees for long-tailed learning under the proposed model.

paragraphs: ProtoPairNet extends case-based neural prediction to continuous outputs. Prototype methods commonly explain classification by comparing an input with representative examples. The paper argues that isolated comparisons lack the directional information needed for regression, where the prediction must express a continuous value rather than select a discrete category.

Its solution uses pairs of prototypes. Predictions depend on the input's relative dissimilarity to the two members, giving the reasoning a geometric interpretation. The architecture bases each prediction on the single most relevant pair instead of drawing on every prototype. This makes the explanation more focused while making the pairwise comparison part of the actual prediction process.

Experiments cover image-based regression and continuous control in reinforcement learning. ProtoPairNet performs comparably to the evaluated black-box models across these tasks. Additional analyses support the meaningfulness of the learned pairs and the faithfulness of their interpretations, while user studies find improved interpretability over existing methods. The results suggest that continuous predictions can retain competitive performance while offering a compact case-based explanation.
neurips-2025-protopairnet-interpretable-.tldr: ProtoPairNet explains continuous predictions through comparison with one relevant prototype pair while matching tested black-box performance.

paragraphs: ProGrad edits a neural network so that its input gradients satisfy specified hard constraints. Gradients describe how outputs respond to input changes, making them relevant to attribution methods and potentially to physical or safety requirements. The paper addresses constraints on these sensitivities, extending the editing problem beyond conditions imposed directly on outputs.

The input to ProGrad includes a network and a collection of inputs paired with linear gradient constraints. It seeks adjusted parameters that satisfy all those supplied constraints while minimizing parameter changes. A new construction called the conditional variable gradient relaxes the NP-hard editing problem into a linear program, allowing an LP solver to perform the constrained edit.

The experiments enforce Grad-CAM constraints on ImageNet ResNet models, Integrated Gradients constraints on Llama 3 and Qwen 3, and gradient constraints in function approximation. The last setting serves as a proxy for safety and physical-invariant applications. The reported results demonstrate hard gradient enforcement in these settings, with the guarantee attached to the supplied input-and-constraint specification.
neurips-2025-provable-gradient-editing-o.tldr: ProGrad uses a linear-programming relaxation to edit network parameters and provably enforce specified linear gradient constraints.

paragraphs: This paper examines whether reasoning models' written chains of thought remain understandable enough to support monitoring. Such monitoring may help reveal intentions or detect problematic behavior, but it depends on reasoning traces being legible and faithful. The study focuses on legibility, including cases where confusing intermediate text precedes a coherent final answer.

Across 14 models, the authors find that R1, R1-Zero, and QwQ often produce traces containing nonsensical phrases, random words, and non-English characters, while Claude models show greater legibility. Within the same training paradigm, larger models tend to produce more illegible reasoning. Illegibility also increases with question difficulty, connecting the problem to more demanding tasks.

In prefill experiments, cutting reasoning off at a legibility threshold reduces accuracy by 53%. This suggests that difficult-to-read portions contribute to performance. The authors discuss possible explanations, including steganography, vestigial tokens, and training artifacts, without establishing one as the cause. The findings raise a qualified concern that chain-of-thought monitoring may become less reliable as outcome-trained models tackle increasingly complex problems.
neurips-2025-reasoning-models-sometimes-.tldr: Some reasoning models produce illegible intermediate text that appears useful for accuracy, potentially weakening chain-of-thought monitoring.

paragraphs: RobotSmith designs tools together with the robot motions needed to use them. The paper motivates this joint problem by noting that human tools can be awkward for robotic manipulators, while template-based design limits possible shapes. Generic 3D generation also does not directly optimize tools for accomplishing manipulation tasks.

The pipeline combines vision-language models' implicit physical knowledge with physics simulation. Collaborative model agents iteratively propose designs, the system generates low-level usage trajectories, and optimization adjusts both tool geometry and how the robot uses it. This connects the tool's form to its practical operation, allowing task performance to guide both parts of the solution.

Evaluation spans manipulation involving rigid objects, deformable objects, and fluids. RobotSmith achieves a reported average success rate of 50.0%, compared with 21.4% for a 3D-generation baseline and 11.1% for tool retrieval. The authors also demonstrate physical deployment, where generated tools and usage plans transfer effectively to real execution. These results support the practicality of jointly designing and learning to operate robotic tools.
neurips-2025-robotsmith-generative-robot.tldr: RobotSmith jointly designs tools and usage motions with vision-language models and simulation, achieving 50.0% average task success.

paragraphs: Aligned-IS addresses a difficulty in watermarking audio produced by next-token prediction models. A watermark may be embedded during generation using discrete audio tokens, but analyzing the resulting audio can produce a different token sequence. This retokenization mismatch makes watermarking techniques adapted from language models harder to detect reliably.

The method groups tokens into clusters and treats tokens in the same cluster equivalently. This changes the watermark's dependence on exact token identity, allowing cluster-level equivalence to counter the mismatch between original and recovered sequences. The design specifically targets the audio setting while retaining the distortion-free character of the watermarking approach.

Tests on prevalent audio-generation platforms show that Aligned-IS preserves generated audio quality and significantly improves watermark detectability relative to the evaluated state-of-the-art distortion-free adaptations. The contribution is therefore a watermarking method built around a concrete obstacle in audio tokenization. Its results support more reliable detection in the tested systems while maintaining the quality of the generated audio.
neurips-2025-robust-distortion-free-wate.tldr: Aligned-IS improves audio watermark detection by treating clustered tokens equivalently to counter retokenization mismatch.

paragraphs: SE-HTGNN learns from graphs that contain different types of entities and change over time. The paper identifies a weakness in approaches that model temporal and spatial information separately: this separation can weaken their interaction while increasing model complexity. Its proposed architecture combines these aspects more directly during representation learning.

A dynamic attention mechanism incorporates temporal modeling into spatial learning. Time information therefore participates in learning graph relationships within the same mechanism. The method also uses large language models to provide prompts that supply prior knowledge about implicit properties of node types. This adds semantic information about the heterogeneous entities alongside the graph's structural and temporal information.

Experiments report speedups of up to tenfold over the compared leading and recent baselines while retaining the best forecasting accuracy in the evaluation. The findings support integrating temporal information into graph attention as a way to reduce complexity without sacrificing predictive quality in these settings. They also demonstrate the proposed combination of graph learning and language-model-derived node-type knowledge.
neurips-2025-simple-and-efficient-hetero.tldr: SE-HTGNN integrates temporal and spatial graph learning, reporting up to tenfold speedups alongside the best evaluated forecasting accuracy.

paragraphs: ConfRover learns both the shapes proteins can adopt and how those shapes change over time. It is trained on molecular dynamics trajectories, which contain sequences of conformations. The paper addresses a divide in earlier generative approaches: some do not explicitly capture temporal dependence, while others cannot directly generate samples independent of time.

The architecture has three modules. An encoder adapted from protein-folding models represents protein-specific information and each frame's conformation in a latent space. A temporal sequence model learns dependencies across frames. An SE(3) diffusion decoder then generates protein structures in continuous space. Together, these components support both individual conformation sampling and time-dependent trajectory generation.

Experiments on ATLAS, a large molecular dynamics dataset containing diverse protein structures, demonstrate learning of conformational dynamics and support for a range of downstream tasks. The authors present ConfRover as the first framework to sample both conformations and trajectories within one model. Its central contribution is this unified treatment of structural variation and temporal evolution from the same trajectory data.
neurips-2025-simultaneous-modeling-of-pr.tldr: ConfRover learns from molecular dynamics data to generate both individual protein conformations and temporally connected trajectories.

paragraphs: Torch-Uncertainty addresses the practical problem of assessing how uncertain a neural network is about its predictions. High predictive performance does not by itself ensure reliable uncertainty estimates. The paper frames this gap as an obstacle to wider use in critical industrial applications, where the reliability of a prediction matters alongside its value.

The contribution is a framework built on PyTorch and Lightning that streamlines training and evaluation with uncertainty-quantification methods. Rather than presenting a single uncertainty estimator, it provides a unified workflow for integrating and examining a diverse set of techniques. This makes the experimental process around uncertainty a central part of the software's purpose.

The paper explains the library's foundational principles and presents extensive benchmark experiments across classification, segmentation, and regression. Covering these task types allows the framework to address uncertainty in several forms of neural prediction. The stated contribution is the shared tooling and comparative experimental coverage; the abstract does not identify one method as universally best. The library is also made publicly available.
neurips-2025-torch-uncertainty-deep-lear.tldr: Torch-Uncertainty provides a unified PyTorch and Lightning workflow for training and benchmarking neural-network uncertainty methods.

paragraphs: RUNC tackles image retrieval queries that combine a reference image with a sentence describing a desired modification. Matching such queries is complicated by semantic overlap among candidate images, noisy annotations, and overconfidence in dominant semantic categories. The paper addresses these sources of uncertainty alongside the problem of combining visual and textual information.

The method uses a high-order conjugate prior distribution to model semantic covariances among candidates and strengthen matching evidence. It estimates an uncertainty coefficient for each candidate, then calibrates the target distribution to encourage more balanced semantic alignment. This links uncertainty estimation directly to the distribution used for learning which images should match.

RUNC also constrains explicit textual embeddings and implicit queries to be orthogonal, aiming to reduce redundant information when forming the combined query. Experiments and ablations on FashionIQ and CIRR support the method's robustness in retrieving reliable matches from large galleries. The contribution combines candidate-level uncertainty calibration with a separate mechanism for making the image-and-text query representation less ambiguous.
neurips-2025-towards-robust-uncertainty-.tldr: RUNC calibrates candidate uncertainty and reduces query redundancy to improve retrieval from combined image-and-text queries.

paragraphs: TransferTraj aims to reuse one vehicle-trajectory model across geographic regions and prediction tasks. Regional differences alter the spatial context and movement patterns found in GPS data, while different tasks require different input and output formats. The paper addresses both obstacles instead of relying only on reusable trajectory embeddings.

For regional transfer, its main learnable module combines spatial, temporal, point-of-interest, and road-network information. A relative-information module represents relationships among spatial features, and a spatial-context mixture of experts handles movement patterns across differing contexts. For task transfer, a common interface expresses tasks through masking and recovering trajectory points and modalities.

That shared interface allows the model to be pretrained once and applied to different tasks without retraining. Experiments use three real-world trajectory datasets and cover task transfer, zero-shot regional transfer, and few-shot regional transfer. The reported results significantly exceed the state-of-the-art baselines across the evaluated scenarios. They support combining context-aware trajectory representations with a unified task format to reduce dependence on specialized regional and task-specific models.
neurips-2025-transfertraj-a-vehicle-traj.tldr: TransferTraj combines regional context modeling with a shared masking-and-recovery interface to transfer across trajectory tasks and regions.
